vignette:
Kwame, a 30-year-old curriculum designer, had been with his partner for nearly two years before the night that reshaped everything. It started when his partner came home already drunk, the sharp smell of alcohol cutting through the apartment. An argument flared over something small-then his partner's voice turned to venom, bringing up Kwame's family in ways that felt engineered to wound. The verbal assault escalated into blows: fists against his ribs, a knee grinding into his back, a pan searing his forearm because the burner had been left on, the burnt smell of scorched metal and skin filling the small kitchen. In that moment Kwame felt a terror he had never known, certain he might not survive. When it was over he lay on the cold floor, shaking, aware of a lingering burnt odour that seemed to coat his skin.

In the weeks after, he ended the relationship but could not end the memory. The pain would return without warning-a sharp ache in his ribs or forearm-as if his body were remembering on its own, bringing back the same full-body terror he had felt pinned to the floor. Sometimes, when he least expected it, he caught the faint burnt or alcohol smell, and the memory would crash over him whole, complete with the helplessness. He started avoiding any situation where he might encounter those smells. At work, designing lesson plans in an open-plan office, a colleague's remark about their own family over lunch left him suddenly stiff, his pulse racing-the sound of the word "family" now acting like a key that unlocked the entire scene. That trigger pulled the memory forward, and in its wake came the old conviction: what happened to him was deeply unfair. No one had been held accountable; he had not even reported it. The injustice burned fresh each time.

The memory itself fuelled those appraisals further. When the pain or terror resurfaced, it did not only replay the event-it made him feel dirty, contaminated, as if the physical contact had left a stain he could not wash off. He had come to believe that the person he had become was unrecognisable from the confident man he used to be. And the cycle tightened: because the memory came with olfactory recollections so vivid-the burnt smell, the alcohol-he began to perceive burnt scents everywhere, in toast at breakfast, in the school's overheated photocopier. Each perceived smell triggered another intrusive memory, another wave of terror and contamination.

A few times he caught himself walking into the teachers' lounge and freezing because someone had left a burner on, even if nothing was actually cooking. He could not explain it to colleagues. He withdrew from any social gathering where people might drink, and when a coworker mentioned their parents over coffee, he made an excuse to leave. His work suffered; he struggled to focus on curriculum drafts, his mind sliding into the same loop. What finally brought him to seek help was the unbearable feeling of being trapped inside his own life: he could not shake the belief that he was permanently changed, that the injustice would never be righted, and that every burnt or alcoholic smell was a warning that he was still in danger. He was most afraid that he would never feel clean again, never feel like himself. But he also hoped, desperately, that a therapist might help him find a way out of the memory's hold.
